title: Closures
summary: A closure is a function bundled with a live reference to its outer scope, kept alive even after that scope would otherwise be discarded. It's the mechanism behind private state, memoization, and the classic loop-variable interview trap.

slides.markdown:
A closure sounds like an advanced concept until you notice you've been relying on one every time you've written a callback that reads a variable from outside itself. That's it — that's a closure.

Formally: a closure is a function paired with a **reference to the scope it was created in**, kept alive for as long as the function itself exists — even after the function that created it has already returned and would otherwise be garbage collected.

This one mechanism explains private state without classes, memoization caches, the `setTimeout`-in-a-loop bug from [execution-context-and-scope](execution-context-and-scope), and a real category of memory leaks. Interviewers ask about it constantly because it's the cleanest test of whether you understand scope as a *live reference*, not a snapshot.

slides.subTitle: A function plus its captured scope

slides.markdown:
Picture two boxes: the outer function's variable environment, and the inner function's code plus a pointer back to that environment. Normally, when the outer function returns, its variable environment has no more references and gets garbage collected.

A closure changes that: the returned inner function still holds a pointer to the outer environment, so the garbage collector can't reclaim it — it's still reachable. The environment isn't copied into the inner function; it's the **same live object**, which is why mutating a closed-over variable from one call is visible on the next.

slides.sectionTitle: Closures vs re-running the outer function
slides.subTitle: One closure per call
slides.markdown:
A recurring misunderstanding: assuming there's "one closure" per function definition. There's one **per call**.

| | `makeCounter()` called once | called twice |
|---|---|---|
| **`count` variables** | one, shared by every call to the returned function | two, completely independent |
| **State sharing** | all calls to the same returned function share it | the two returned functions never see each other's state |

```javascript
const counterA = makeCounter();
const counterB = makeCounter();
counterA(); // 1
counterA(); // 2
counterB(); // 1 — a separate count, unaffected by counterA
```

Each invocation of the outer function creates a brand-new variable environment, so each closure you return is capturing its **own** copy, not a shared global. This is exactly what makes the factory pattern (`makeCounter`, `memoize`, custom hooks) safe to call more than once.
